newsitem.title: USA: Republicans urge White House to cut more spending.
newsitem.headline: Republicans urge White House to cut more spending.

text.p: Republican budget leaders on Wednesday called on the White House to come up with greater cuts in domestic spending and said they found no movement from the administration towards compromise in the second day of budget talks.

Congressional sources said the administration backed down on offering deeper domestic spending cuts after running into opposition from House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri about Medicare cuts presented Tuesday.
Democratic aides said Gephardt was "furious" that he had not been notified of the cuts and felt the White House was willing to cut Medicare too deeply.

After three hours of closed-door meetings centering on domestic programs ranging from education to national parks, Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici of New Mexico summed up the day as "sort of the darkness before the dawn," and his Democratic counterpart, Sen Frank Lautenberg told reporters, "Today was a cold shower kind of day."

The outcome was in sharp contrast to the upbeat news conference a day earlier after the administration offered to reduce Medicare by another $18 billion over five years to hit a goal of slowing growth in the program by $100 bilion.

Still, House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, Republican of Ohio, said more needed to be trimmed from Medicare and other entitlements if they are to reach a deal to balance the federal budget by 2002.
Republicans have said they are giving the talks until the middle of next week to yield an agreement before they move ahead with a separate plan in concert with conservative Democrats.

Office of Management and Budget Director Frank Raines, who has pledged to hold his negotiating cards close to the vest, declined to discuss the White House budget proposal. "We are not goign to get into what we did or didn't do. We did have a very good, frank discussion about one of the toughest areas we are going to have to tackle," he said.
Republicans asked the White House to return in a few days with a list of priority programs and spending levels that would be acceptable to them.
But as Kasich of Ohio noted, the spending cuts in domestic programs are unlikely to please either side. "The administration's not going to be happy, we're not going to be happy," he said.

Republicans have criticized the administration for putting off for three years most spending cuts in these domestic programs -- which pay for about one-sixth of the government and must be approved each year. The White House proposed spending more in the coming 1998 fiscal year for education, training, the environment, health and law enforcement.
Lautenberg, a New Jersey Democrat, said he sensed a willingness on both sides to work through the difficult stretch and expected the White House might move down on its domestic spending number.
The talks are to continue Thursday on tax proposals and negotiators will move to other topics Friday and Monday.
